title: Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy
outcomes: Describe the strategic role of the CFO.
Relate strategy levels to financial planning.
Explain the interface of financial policy and strategy.
Compute sustainable growth and external funding requirements.

meta.exam_tip: For growth questions, compute SGR first, then EFR, then suggest the levers.

concepts.title: The strategic role of the CFO
body: The modern CFO is a strategic partner, not just a record keeper: involved in capital allocation, risk management, investor relations, funding strategy, mergers and restructuring, technology and data in finance, and governance and compliance.
The CFO links business plans to their financial consequences — testing whether strategies create value, whether they can be funded, and how they affect risk and returns.

Strategic financial management means managing finance with long-term goals in mind: deciding investments, financing and dividend policy so as to maximise shareholder wealth while handling uncertainty.
concepts.analogy: The CFO turns strategy into numbers and numbers into strategy.
concepts.work: A CFO tests whether an expansion plan earns more than its cost of capital before funding it.

concepts.title: Strategy levels and financial planning
body: Strategy works at three levels: corporate (which businesses to be in and how to allocate resources across them), business unit (how to compete in a given market — cost leadership, differentiation, focus) and functional (how finance, marketing, operations and HR support the business strategy).
Financial planning translates strategy into money terms: forecasting sales, assets, funds needed and sources, with targets for profitability, liquidity and solvency.
Good financial plans set clear objectives, consider alternative scenarios, stay flexible, and are reviewed regularly against actual results.
concepts.analogy: Corporate picks the field, business unit picks the game plan, functions carry it out.
concepts.work: Finance at the functional level arranges working capital for a new product launch.

concepts.title: Linking financial policy and corporate strategy
body: Financial policy covers the investment, financing and dividend decisions, plus policies on liquidity, risk and capital structure. These must fit the corporate strategy: an aggressive growth strategy needs funding and risk policies that support it.

Strategy often depends on finance: limited funds can force a firm to grow slower, sell non-core assets, form alliances or raise outside capital. Conversely, financial policy should be shaped by strategic priorities, not the other way round.
Key interface areas include the sources and cost of finance, investment selection, dividend and retention policy, and managing financial risks so that strategic plans are not derailed.
concepts.analogy: Strategy and finance must agree — or the plan fails on paper or on the ground.
concepts.work: A firm planning acquisitions keeps borrowing capacity in reserve.

concepts.title: Sustainable growth and external funding needs
body: The sustainable growth rate (SGR) is the fastest sales growth a firm can achieve without issuing new equity, while keeping its capital structure and payout ratio constant: SGR = ROE × retention ratio (1 − payout). ROE itself depends on profit margin, asset turnover and leverage.

If planned growth exceeds the SGR, the firm must raise equity, increase leverage, cut dividends, or improve margins and asset efficiency — or slow growth. If actual growth is below SGR, surplus cash can be returned to shareholders, used to reduce debt or deployed in acquisitions. Inflation raises funding needs and so lowers effective sustainable growth.

External funding requirement (EFR) = increase in assets needed − increase in spontaneous liabilities − retained earnings, assuming assets and spontaneous liabilities move with sales. A negative EFR indicates surplus funds.
concepts.analogy: SGR tells you how fast you can grow on your own; EFR tells you how much money you will need.
concepts.work: At 20% ROE and 60% retention, a firm can grow 12% a year without new shares.

illustrations.title: How fast can we grow without new equity?
illustrations.q: Nimbus Ltd. earns profit after tax of ₹30 crore on equity of ₹150 crore and pays dividends of ₹12 crore. It wants to keep its debt-equity ratio and payout ratio unchanged and issue no new shares. Compute its sustainable growth rate. Sales are expected to grow 15% next year — what does that imply?

Working
Result
rows: Needs more debt, new equity, lower payout or better margins/turnover
solution.title: SGR = ROE × retention

illustrations.title: External funding requirement
illustrations.q: Sales of Orchid Ltd. are ₹1,000 crore and will rise to ₹1,200 crore. Assets of ₹800 crore and spontaneous liabilities (creditors, accruals) of ₹200 crore move in line with sales. Net margin is 10% and 60% of profit is retained. Compute the external funding requirement.

viva.model: The highest sales growth a firm can fund using retained earnings alone, with no fresh share issue, keeping its leverage and payout ratio constant; it equals ROE times the retention ratio.
Increase in assets needed minus increase in spontaneous liabilities minus retained earnings of the year.

viva.q: What are the three levels of strategy?
viva.model: Corporate, business unit and functional level strategy.

viva.q: How should financial policy relate to corporate strategy?
viva.model: It should support and fit the strategy, while finance constraints also shape what strategies are feasible.

viva.q: What can a firm do when growth is below its SGR?
viva.model: Return surplus cash through dividends or buybacks, repay debt, or invest in acquisitions.
